input:
This report presents an energy assessment of a dairy plant, covering the current use of energy at the site, the refrigeration system, the steam system, and a recommendation arising from the assessment. The assessment has been carried out on the basis of the records available at the site, and its findings are set out in the sections that follow, taken in turn.

Current use

Electricity is the principal energy stream covered by this assessment, and the site currently uses 2854 MWh of electricity per year. The assessment has examined how this electricity is used across the plant, and refrigeration accounts for the largest share of the total. The remainder is spread across the processing operations, the cleaning of the plant, and the general services that support production, and no single one of these approaches the refrigeration share. The pattern of use follows the pattern of production, and the refrigeration load is present whenever product is being handled or held at temperature, which at this site is effectively continuous. It is also worth observing that the demand for refrigeration does not switch off when production pauses, since product that has been made still has to be held at temperature, and this gives the site a substantial baseline of consumption that continues around the clock, in quiet periods as well as in busy ones.

Refrigeration

Refrigeration is the largest single use of electricity at the plant, and it is therefore the natural focus of the assessment. The refrigeration system holds the product and the cold stores at temperature, and in doing so it rejects heat at its condensers. This rejected heat is currently lost to the surroundings, even though the plant also has a substantial demand for heated water for processing and for cleaning. Recovering the heat that the refrigeration system rejects, and putting it to work where heated water is needed, is the opportunity that the assessment identifies. The heat is available whenever the refrigeration plant is running, which matches well with the continuous character of the site's demand for hot water, although the detailed matching of the two has not been examined at this stage. The opportunity is, in a sense, a matter of putting two existing features of the plant together: a system that is continuously rejecting heat, and a set of duties that are continuously asking for it. Schemes of this general kind are well established in the food industry, where large refrigeration plants and a constant demand for hot water are so often found side by side on the same site.

Steam

Steam serves the heating duties of the plant, including the heat treatment of the product and the cleaning of the equipment. It should be noted that the steam figures available to this assessment are drawn from one winter month only. Winter is a period of high heating demand, and a single winter month cannot be taken as representative of the year as a whole. For that reason, the steam figures are reported here as they stand for that month, and they have not been extended or annualised in any way. Any conclusion that depends on steam use over a full year would need figures from a longer period, and the recommendation below is framed with that limitation in mind. None of this means that the steam figures are of no use: they describe the month they cover, and they are the best information available for that month. It does mean, however, that they have to be handled with care, and that any attempt to build a picture of the whole year upon them would risk seriously misleading the reader.

Recommendation

It is recommended that a heat-recovery retrofit be installed on the refrigeration system, and the site engineering manager would own the retrofit. The retrofit is projected to save 19% of electricity use, which corresponds to a derived saving of 542 MWh per year. The capital cost of the retrofit is $286k. At an electricity price of $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $65071, and the derived simple payback on the investment is 4.4 years. Overall, the assessment considers this to be an attractive opportunity, since the largest use of electricity on the site is also the source of the recovered heat. It is nevertheless important to remember that the steam figures behind parts of the assessment are seasonal, being drawn from one winter month, and this flag should be kept in mind when the recommendation is considered. The payback quoted is a simple payback, and it takes no account of the timing of the savings beyond the year in which they arise, which is the conventional treatment at the assessment stage and is appropriate to a decision of this size.

A heat-recovery retrofit on the refrigeration system is recommended. The site engineering manager owns the retrofit.

Current use

The site uses 2854 MWh of electricity per year. Refrigeration takes the largest share of that use. The remaining electricity serves the processing operations, the cleaning of the plant, and the general services that support production; no one of these approaches the refrigeration share. Use follows production, and the refrigeration load runs whenever product is handled or held at temperature, which at this site is effectively continuous. The assessment works from the electricity record for the year; it does not re-measure the individual loads, and the split of the remainder between the smaller uses is stated qualitatively because the record supports the ranking, not a finer division. The year's figure is a total, and the assessment takes it as the base for the recommendation. Loads that run with production rise and fall with the production rate; the holding load does not, and the holding load is what keeps the baseline of use high between campaigns and outside production hours. Electricity is also the stream on which a change shows soonest: it is metered for the site as a whole, and a change in it is visible in the record without a special measurement campaign.

Refrigeration

Refrigeration is the largest use because the plant holds product and cold stores at temperature without interruption. The system rejects heat at its condensers, and that heat is currently lost to the surroundings. The plant also heats water for processing and for cleaning, and the demand for heated water runs across the same hours as the refrigeration load. The retrofit recovers heat from the condenser side of the refrigeration system and delivers it to the water-heating duties. The source and the demand are both continuous, and the recovery does not depend on storage to bridge a gap between them. The detailed matching of the recovered heat to each water-heating duty is design work; the assessment establishes the size of the source and the existence of the demand, and the recommendation is sized on the electricity the refrigeration system uses. The retrofit is an exchanger and a circulating loop on the condenser side. The refrigeration system itself is unchanged and continues to do its own duty; the retrofit takes heat the condensers reject in any case. The condenser heat is low-grade heat, and its value depends on the temperature the water-heating duties accept: duties that take warm water absorb more of it than duties that need the highest temperatures. The assessment does not grade the duties, and the grading belongs to the design stage named in the recommendation.

Steam

Steam serves the heating duties of the plant, including the heat treatment of the product and the cleaning of the equipment. The steam figures available to the assessment come from one winter month. A winter month is a high-demand month for heating, and it does not represent the year. The figures are therefore reported as they stand for that month and are not extended to a yearly figure anywhere in this assessment. No part of the recommendation is sized on the steam figures, and a decision that turned on yearly steam use would need a longer record before it could be taken. The flag is a limit on the use of the figures, not a defect in them: for the month they describe, they are the record of what the plant used. A full year of steam figures, set beside the production record for the same year, is what an annual steam balance would need, and collecting that year is a matter of time rather than of new instrumentation.

Recommendation

Install the heat-recovery retrofit on the refrigeration system. The site engineering manager owns the retrofit. The retrofit is projected to save 19% of electricity use, a derived saving of 542 MWh per year. The capital cost is $286k. At $0.12 per kWh the derived annual saving is $65071, and the derived simple payback is 4.4 years. The payback rests on the electricity record for the year and on the projected saving; the saving is a projection, not a measured result, and the first year of operation is the test of it. The steam figures behind the wider assessment are seasonal, drawn from one winter month, and that flag stands on the recommendation as it does on the steam section. The projection is stated on electricity alone. Any effect of the retrofit on steam use stands outside the payback as calculated, in either direction, because the steam record does not support a yearly figure against which to state it. A reader who took the steam figures as yearly figures would misjudge the balance of the plant, and the flag is repeated at the decision point to prevent exactly that reading of them. Next step: the site engineering manager takes the retrofit to detailed design, where the matching of recovered heat to the water-heating duties is fixed.
